items.title: Democratic Voters Debate What’s Wrong With the Party | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Democrats are on track to make gains in the November midterm elections, but they’re benefiting from President Trump’s unpopularity—not their own party’s image. In fact, Democrats have received some of their lowest approval ratings ever since Trump took office last year. 

Democratic voters are divided over what they believe their party should stand for and who is best equipped to beat Republicans. The party’s far-left flank has been ascendent with members of the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressives toppling longtime incumbents in some party primaries. For the first time ever, several highly competitive Senate and House seats will have far-left candidates as the Democratic nominees—a test of progressive power in competitive races. 

We asked a group of Democratic voters from across the country to join us to talk about the party at this moment. Watch the video to learn more. 

In the coming weeks we will have a video discussion with young men who voted for Trump in 2024. A year ago we spoke to a group of them to get their read on Trump’s first six months in office. We brought them back together to see how they feel about the administration now.

1:22 Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries

items.title: How Arc’teryx Became a $2B+ Luxury Brand Without Intending To | WSJ The Economics Of
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>A $900 Arc’teryx Alpha SV jacket has more than 150 component parts from more than 35 suppliers. The highly technical products are designed for climbers, but the rapid brand growth has also been fueled by “gorpcore,” a fashion trend where technical gear is worn as high-end streetwear. 

WSJ got rare access inside Arc’teryx’s Canadian manufacturing facility ARC’One to learn how the company carved out a unique brand identity in an industry dominated by mainstream giants like Patagonia and The North Face.

items.title: Miami-Dade Voted for Trump. How Do Voters Feel About Him Now? | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Florida’s most populous county, Miami-Dade is roughly 70% Hispanic. Two-thirds speak Spanish at home. More than 50% are immigrants. And about one-third are Cuban. In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to flip Miami-Dade County since 1988. 

With the 2026 midterms quickly approaching, WSJ’s Sabrina Rodriguez returns home to Miami for a mood check: Two years into Trump’s second term, how are Miami residents feeling about his handling of the economy and immigration? Are they motivated to turn out in November?

items.title: Evan Gershkovich on What Life Inside Russia’s Prison System Was Like | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>When Evan Gershkovich was arrested by Russia’s security forces in 2023—the first U.S. journalist charged with espionage in the country since the Cold War—he never stopped reporting.

Now, sitting down with Evan ahead of the release of his book, “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” WSJ editor in chief Emma Tucker listened as he recalled the “pure fear” of his arrest—and how he survived over a year in Moscow’s infamous Lefortovo prison.

items.title: Inside the School Where Teens Do Farmwork for $40K a Semester
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>At the Mountain School, families pay $40,000 a semester for their teens to do chores on a farm in rural Vermont. Their goal: Students learn to appreciate the people doing these tasks in every community.⁠
⁠
Some students and alums consider the Mountain School a secret path to top colleges. Other families are seeking a wider perspective beyond traditional schooling and a rare reprieve from technology.⁠

#Vermont #Farm #WSJ</article>

items.title: How a Speed Boat Carries $200M of Cocaine Into Europe | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Drug traffickers are switching up their tactics to import record amounts of cocaine into Europe. Instead of smuggling the drug in massive shipping containers at major ports, they’re increasingly relying on swarms of high-speed boats known locally as narcolanchas.

WSJ explains how drug traffickers can spend weeks at sea aboard the superfast vessels and how Spanish customs agents are struggling to hunt them down.
